title: The Horse That Fooled the Experts
style: in a calm, dry, deadpan documentary voice, at a brisk and lively pace with only short pauses between sentences

beats.vo: In 1904, a team of German experts tested a horse that could do math. And they agreed: he really could.
It's Berlin, and a math teacher named Wilhelm von Osten has spent years giving school lessons to his horse, Hans.
Ask Hans what three plus two is, and he taps his hoof. Five times.
Soon he's doing fractions, telling the time, and even spelling out names.
Crowds pour into the courtyard, and von Osten never charges them a single coin.
So thirteen experts show up: teachers, a vet, a cavalry officer, a circus manager, and the director of the Berlin Zoo.
In September 1904, they announce there's no trick at all.
Then a psychologist named Oskar Pfungst tries something new. He asks questions he doesn't know the answer to.
When Hans could see someone who knew the answer, he was right eighty-nine percent of the time. When he couldn't, six percent.
Hans wasn't counting. He was watching. As his taps got close to the answer, people tensed up, and on the right tap they relaxed. So Hans stopped.
Luckily, nobody was cheating. Unluckily, that included von Osten, who never believed a word of it.
It's like a friend guessing your card, because your face lights up the moment they touch it.
Today it's called the Clever Hans effect, and it's why experiments are run double-blind.
It has even been caught in drug-sniffing dogs, and in artificial intelligence.
Hans never learned to count to five. But he could read thirteen experts like a book.

caption: In 1904, thirteen experts agreed a horse could do math. Then one psychologist asked a better question. #history #cleverhans #psychology #didyouknow #animation
